clinicalPearls: Rare systemic disease defined by recurrent inflammation of cartilaginous structures, with the ears, nose, respiratory tract, and joints as hallmark sites; the eyes, inner ear, nervous system, skin, and cardiovascular system may also be involved (p.2917).

Ear involvement is the most common manifestation, affecting roughly 80-90% of patients, and typically spares the non-cartilaginous lobule; pain may occur with minimal visible swelling or erythema (p.2918).

Triggers for ear pain often include minor trauma (lying on the affected side, wearing glasses) or temperature change; 'cauliflower ear' from cartilage damage occurs only in a small subset after recurrent episodes (p.2918).

Nasal disease often presents as a pressure sensation at the bridge of the nose; a saddle-nose deformity may develop but is not universal, and unlike GPA the nasal perforations in RP are usually anterior rather than septal (p.2918-2919).

Airway involvement such as subglottic stenosis may be misdiagnosed as adult-onset asthma; severe narrowing can cause stridor and is a medical emergency, and chronic damage can lead to tracheomalacia, bronchomalacia, or tracheal calcification (p.2919).

Costochondral joint inflammation can produce severe bilateral chest pain that is reproducible on palpation and not movement-related, sometimes mimicking acute coronary syndrome and prompting emergency evaluation (p.2919-2920).

Recurrent chondritis of the ears and nose in older male patients with severe systemic inflammation and progressive bone marrow failure should prompt evaluation for VEXAS syndrome (somatic UBA1 mutation) (p.2917, 2920).
Episcleritis is the most frequent ocular manifestation; scleritis is rare but warrants urgent ophthalmologic evaluation given the risk of vision loss, scleromalacia, or globe rupture (p.2920).

Because disease activity is intermittent and patients may appear non-inflamed during a clinic visit, a longitudinal history and review of patient-provided photographs are essential to diagnosis (p.2918).

MAGIC syndrome (mouth and genital ulcers with inflamed cartilage) overlaps with Behcet's syndrome features such as pathergy and GI involvement and may include large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta (p.2920).
Some patients carry concurrent rheumatologic diagnoses such as Sjogren's syndrome or systemic lupus erythematosus (p.2917).
Neurologic attribution to RP is a diagnosis of exclusion; infection and malignancy must be ruled out first, though encephalitis and meningitis can occur in RP (p.2920).
harrison.pathophysiology: The exact mechanisms remain unclear despite study of genetic, environmental, and immunologic factors. Limited animal-model data suggest autoimmunity against cartilage components may contribute: immunizing certain animals against type II collagen, type IX collagen, or matrilin-1 can reproduce aspects of the human phenotype. However, autoantibodies (including anti-type II collagen) are neither sensitive nor specific enough for diagnosis, and observational data showing B-cell-depleting therapy is not particularly effective argue against a dominant antibody-mediated mechanism. Proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines linked to both innate and adaptive immunity have been associated with RP but are inconsistent. Histologically, acute cartilage shows a mixed myeloid and lymphoid inflammatory infiltrate at the cartilage interface; over time there is lacunar breakdown, loss of chondrocytes, and replacement by fibrosis (p.2918).
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) - distinguished by ANCA positivity and glomerulonephritis, which are not features of RP (p.2920)
VEXAS syndrome - especially in older males with cytopenia, macrocytosis, and lymphopenia (p.2920)
Rheumatoid arthritis - the small-joint pattern can mimic RA but RP arthritis is nonerosive and nondeforming (p.2919)
Behcet's syndrome - overlap via MAGIC syndrome (p.2920)
Adult-onset asthma - airway chondritis is frequently misattributed to asthma (p.2919)
infectionMimics: Infectious diseases of the external ear mimicking ear chondritis (p.2920)
Infectious airway disease mimicking airway chondritis (p.2920)
nonInfectiousMimics: Traumatic otohematoma and red ear syndrome (ear) (p.2920)
Cutaneous diseases of the external ear (p.2920)
Traumatic airway stenosis and congenital airway disorders (p.2920)
additionalInvestigations: Audiometry to assess for conductive and sensorineural hearing loss in all suspected patients (p.2920)
Dynamic expiratory-phase chest CT to evaluate tracheobronchomalacia (p.2920)
Direct laryngoscopy to visualize upper-airway cartilage damage; bronchoscopy of the lower airway can exacerbate disease and must be used with caution (p.2920-2921)
Echocardiography to assess valvular heart disease (p.2921)
FDG-PET to detect inflammation in large arteries and larger airways (p.2921)
Vestibular testing (finger-to-nose, Romberg, nystagmus) when dizziness is present (p.2920)
Genetic testing for UBA1 and bone marrow assessment for VEXAS in older males with cytopenias (p.2920)
Cartilage biopsy reserved for excluding mimics (infection, malignancy) since findings are nonspecific (p.2918, 2921)
redFlags: Stridor from severe airway/subglottic narrowing - a medical emergency requiring urgent attention to avoid mortality (p.2919)
Features of scleritis - urgent ophthalmology referral due to risk of vision loss, scleromalacia, or globe rupture (p.2920)
Cytopenia with macrocytosis and lymphopenia in older males - suggests VEXAS and possible progressive bone marrow failure (p.2917, 2920)
Severe costochondral chest pain that can mimic acute coronary syndrome (p.2919-2920)
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes depend heavily on organ involvement. Airway disease can progress to tracheomalacia, bronchomalacia, or tracheal calcification, and severe subglottic narrowing carries mortality risk. Scleritis can lead to vision loss or globe rupture. VEXAS-associated disease involves progressive bone marrow failure and is potentially life-threatening, so prompt recognition is essential. Acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP) are not reliably elevated, so they cannot be used to gauge severity (p.2917-2920).
pitfalls: Airway involvement is commonly misdiagnosed as adult-onset asthma, delaying treatment and risking chronic large-airway damage (p.2919)
Normal ESR and CRP do not exclude active RP, as acute-phase reactants are not reliably elevated (p.2918)
There is no diagnostic blood or tissue biomarker; relying on a single test is a pitfall - diagnosis rests on clinical pattern recognition over time (p.2918, 2920)
Cartilage biopsy yields nonspecific findings and can cause morbidity; it should not be expected to confirm RP (p.2918, 2921)
Patients may appear non-inflamed at a single visit because disease activity is intermittent (p.2918)
Published diagnostic criteria were derived from small cohorts, are largely expert-opinion-based, and have not been formally validated (p.2920)
Assuming a saddle nose implies GPA - in RP the deformity usually lacks septal perforation (perforations are anterior) (p.2918-2919)
harrison.severityClassification: No formally validated severity grading exists. Several diagnostic schemes have been proposed: McAdam's criteria require 3 of 6 features (bilateral auricular chondritis, nonerosive seronegative inflammatory polyarthritis, nasal chondritis, ocular inflammation, respiratory-tract chondritis, vestibular/cochlear dysfunction); the Damiani-Levine modification accepts 3 clinical features, or 1 feature plus histologic chondritis, or 2 features plus clinical response to treatment; Michet's criteria use 3 major criteria (ear, nose, or respiratory-tract inflammation) and 4 minor criteria (ocular inflammation, hearing loss, vestibular dysfunction, seronegative inflammatory arthritis), requiring 2 major or 1 major plus 2 minor. All are limited by lack of precise organ-involvement definitions (p.2920).
management: Systemic corticosteroids are the mainstay for active chondritis, given at higher doses for organ-threatening flares and tapered to the lowest effective maintenance dose
Add steroid-sparing immunosuppression such as methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate for persistent or relapsing disease
Consider biologic therapy, including TNF inhibitors or tocilizumab, for refractory or severe airway and ocular involvement
NSAIDs or short steroid courses for isolated auricular, nasal or costochondral inflammation, with analgesia and protection of inflamed cartilage from minor trauma

Treat threatened airway as an emergency, with securing of the airway and consideration of stenting, positive-pressure support or tracheostomy for severe subglottic stenosis, tracheomalacia or bronchomalacia
Structured surveillance for organ complications with audiometry, echocardiography and dynamic expiratory chest CT, and urgent ophthalmology review for scleritis
Refer to rheumatology within a multidisciplinary team, and investigate for VEXAS syndrome or occult malignancy in older men or atypical, treatment-resistant disease
